name: 3D Printers
lead: Creality Ender-3 S1 — two FDM printers for prototypes, props and tactile resources
caption: One of the two Ender-3 S1 printers, with sample prints and filament on the shelf.
summary: Desktop 3D printers that build objects layer by layer from plastic filament. Students and researchers design a model (or download one), prepare it in a slicer and print it in minutes to hours. In an education lab the printers turn ideas into tangible things: tactile maps and letters, game pieces, replicas of cultural objects, phone stands, spare parts for other equipment.
kit: with direct-drive extruder and automatic bed levelling
220 × 220 × 270 mm; PLA, PETG and TPU filament
Creality Print, Ultimaker Cura or PrusaSlicer; models from Thingiverse or Printables
teaching: molecules, cells, terrain, historical artefacts and geometric solids students can hold.
students identify a real problem and print a prototype solution.
tactile diagrams, maps and graphs for learners with visual impairments.
fraction bars, tiles, game pieces and models made for a specific lesson.
research: what changes when students design and fabricate their own learning objects.
physical models and conceptual understanding in STEM.
printing mounts, stands and parts for study setups.
notes: The nozzle and bed get hot; supervise students and let prints cool before removing them.
Print with PLA in a ventilated room; store filament dry.
Prepare models in Creality Print, Cura or PrusaSlicer before printing.

name: Cricut Maker 3
lead: Computer-controlled cutting machine — vinyl, paper, card, fabric and more
caption: The Cricut Maker 3 (model CXPL303) on the lab bench.
summary: A precision cutting plotter: you design shapes, letters or layouts in the Cricut Design Space app, and the machine cuts, scores, draws or engraves them on hundreds of materials — from sticker vinyl and cardstock to fabric, leather and thin wood. It is the quickest route from a digital design to a physical label, stencil, sticker, card or tactile material.
kit: (model CXPL303) with fine-point blade and accessories
Cricut Design Space (Windows, macOS, iOS, Android)
teaching: labels, stencils, manipulatives, word walls and signage.
posters, packaging, infographics and paper engineering such as pop-up models.
textured shapes, raised labels and large-print materials.
displays for science fairs, showcases and poster sessions.
research: how pre-service teachers use fabrication tools to design materials.
iterating on teacher-made materials with students.
notes: Design Space needs an account; the machine connects by USB or Bluetooth.
Choose the right material setting before each cut — the wrong one tears paper or leaves vinyl uncut.
Keep spare mats and a selection of vinyl and cardstock in the lab.

name: Green Screen Studio Kit
lead: Pull-up chroma-key backdrop, two LED panels and a tripod — a small video studio that packs away
caption: The kit set up in the lab: Emart pull-up green screen, two UBeesize LED panels and the Victiv NT70 tripod.
summary: Everything needed to film someone in front of a background that is replaced later: a green backdrop that pulls up from its case and locks at the height you want, two LED panels to light the screen and the speaker evenly, and a tripod that holds a camera or a phone. Recorded clips go into a chroma-key app or editor (Do Ink, iMovie, CapCut, OBS) that swaps the green for any image or video — a newsroom, a map, a slide, a historical site.
kit: — pull-up backdrop with a self-locking frame, stores in its own case
— aluminium, about 50–188 cm (19.5–74 in), pan head, phone holder and quick-release plate
the camera or phone and the editing software
teaching: students present a science topic, a historical event or a current issue in front of a map or scene.
short how-to and explainer clips with slides or diagrams behind the presenter.
students “stand” in a place they researched and explain it.
recorded talks that students review with a rubric before presenting live.
pre-service teachers record micro-lessons for peer feedback.
research: producing consistent stimuli for multimedia-learning studies.
what learners do with authoring tools when they produce rather than watch.
notes: Light the green screen evenly first, then the speaker; shadows and wrinkles are what break the key.
Keep the speaker about a metre in front of the screen and avoid green clothing.

name: Insta360 X5
lead: 8K 360° action camera — Essentials Bundle with spare battery and invisible selfie stick
caption: The Insta360 X5 Essentials Bundle.
summary: A pocket camera with two lenses that records everything around it at once, in up to 8K 360° video. Afterwards you either keep the full sphere — to watch in a VR headset like our Quest 3 or on YouTube 360 — or “reframe” it into a normal video, choosing where to look after the fact. The selfie stick disappears from the shot, it is waterproof and rugged, and stabilisation keeps the footage smooth while walking.
kit: — dual 1/1.28-inch sensors, 8K30 360° video, 72 MP photos, removable lens guards
spare battery, fast-charge case, 114 cm invisible selfie stick, lens guard, lens cap and carry case
Insta360 app (phone) and Insta360 Studio (computer) for reframing and export
teaching: students film a place — a lab, a museum, a natural site — and build a guided 360° tour with questions for viewers.
future teachers revisit a lesson in 360° and notice what a fixed camera would miss.
record scenes to view on the Quest 3 instead of buying ready-made content.
groups act out a situation around the camera; others watch and discuss how they would respond.
research: noticing, presence and reflection compared with standard video.
recording whole environments for later analysis.
notes: Keep people within one to two metres of the camera and avoid rotating it while filming — viewers in headsets feel it.
Filming people in public or in class needs consent; 360° means everyone in the room is in the shot.

name: littleBits Kits
lead: Gizmos & Gadgets Kit (2015) and Code Kit (2017) — snap-together electronics
caption: The two littleBits boxes: Gizmos & Gadgets and the Code Kit.
summary: littleBits are small electronic modules — power, sensors, motors, lights, buzzers — that snap together with magnets, so students can build working circuits and inventions in minutes without soldering or wiring. The Gizmos & Gadgets Kit focuses on mechanical inventions (materials for 12 projects with 15 bits); the Code Kit adds a programmable “codeBit” and over 100 classroom activities with 10 lessons for grades 3 and up.
kit: 100+ activities and 10 lessons; 1–3 students per kit; grades 3+
teaching: “build something that helps…” prompts in any subject, followed by a short pitch.
inputs, outputs and feedback made visible in a working circuit.
circuits, energy and simple machines through hands-on builds.
quick mock-ups of interactive objects in design-thinking sessions.
research: observing idea generation with modular, no-wiring electronics.
physical computing with younger learners in grades 3–6.
notes: Bits snap together with magnets and only connect the right way round — no wiring, no soldering.
Build in order: power first, then inputs, then outputs.
The two kits can be combined for bigger inventions.

name: Meeting Owl 4+
lead: Owl Labs 360° camera, microphone and speaker for hybrid classes and meetings
caption: The Meeting Owl 4+ with its reference card on the lab table.
summary: An all-in-one device that sits in the middle of the table and gives remote participants a sense of being in the room. It shows a 360° panorama of everyone present and automatically switches a second view to whoever is speaking. It connects to a computer by USB-C and works as camera, microphone and speaker in Zoom, Teams, Google Meet and other platforms. It does not record on its own — recording happens in the meeting software.
kit: — 4K 360° camera (64 MP sensor), microphones and speakers in one unit
Meeting Owl app for settings and updates; any video-conferencing platform
teaching: bring a remote expert or a partner class into a round-table discussion.
joint sessions with a class at another school or university.
pre-service teachers lead a small-group activity while observers watch remotely.
research: record group discussions with every participant in frame (with consent), via the meeting software.
participation and turn-taking between in-room and remote students.
the 360° view keeps gaze and gesture of all participants available for analysis.
notes: Place it in the centre of the table, at least 0.5 m (18 in) from the screen.
In the meeting software, set camera, microphone and speaker all to Meeting Owl.
Tell participants when a session is being recorded.

name: Meta Quest 3
lead: Standalone VR and mixed-reality headset — 512 GB, four units for group sessions
caption: A Quest 3 headset with its two Touch Plus controllers.
summary: A self-contained headset — no PC or cables needed — for virtual reality and mixed reality, where virtual objects appear in the real room through colour passthrough cameras. Users explore 3D environments, visit virtual places, use creative and educational apps, and meet others in shared spaces. With four units, small groups can be in the same virtual room at once.
kit: Meta Horizon store and app; can also stream PC VR over Wi-Fi
teaching: museums, historical sites, outer space or the inside of the human body.
lab procedures, safety training, clinical or workplace scenarios that are hard to stage in class.
3D models in geometry, anatomy, architecture and geography.
3D drawing, sculpting and storytelling apps, followed by a reflection task.
research: retention and transfer after VR compared with video or text.
onboarding, comfort, motion sickness and accessibility.
behaviour and decision-making in controlled virtual scenarios.
how immersion shapes engagement and learning.
notes: Keep sessions to 15–20 minutes at first and clear a 2 × 2 m area per headset.
Clean the facial interface after each user; disposable covers help in group sessions.
Each headset needs its account and apps ready before a group session.

name: micro:bit Smart Cutebot
lead: ELECFREAKS robot car driven by a micro:bit — block coding on wheels
caption: One of the three Cutebot cars, assembled and sitting on its box.
summary: A small two-wheeled robot car controlled by a BBC micro:bit. Students program it in MakeCode (drag-and-drop blocks or Python) to drive, follow lines, avoid obstacles with its ultrasonic sensor, light up its LEDs and react to the micro:bit's buttons and sensors. It is one of the quickest ways to get from “first line of code” to something that moves across the floor.
kit: with two motors, line-tracking sensors, ultrasonic distance sensor, RGB headlights and a buzzer
slots into the top of the car and is programmed over USB or Bluetooth
Microsoft MakeCode in the browser, with the Cutebot extension
teaching: drive the car with block code, then add sensors one at a time.
students write step-by-step instructions for a partner to turn into code.
distance, speed, angles and timing become concrete problems.
the robot navigates a map of a story, a city, an ecosystem or a cell.
line-following races, obstacle courses and delivery missions.
research: recording and analysing group talk during debugging.
pre-service teachers' confidence with physical computing.
notes: Each car runs on 3 AAA batteries.
MakeCode runs in any browser, so a first session can start on a laptop before the cars come out.
Line following works best on a light floor or paper with a clear dark line.

name: Nezha Inventor's Kit for micro:bit
lead: ELECFREAKS building-block kit with motors and sensors — medium difficulty
caption: The three Nezha kits in their carrying cases.
summary: A construction kit that combines a micro:bit with plastic building blocks, servo motors and sensors. Students build mechanical models — vehicles, cranes, a catapult, a smart lamp — and then program their behaviour in MakeCode. It sits one step above the Cutebot: more building, more parts, more room for open-ended projects.
kit: with motor and servo ports and a rechargeable battery
as the controller; programmed in MakeCode
teaching: each group builds and programs a different model and presents it to the class.
students write, test and revise assembly instructions for others.
plan, build, test, improve — with the robot as the evidence.
simple machines, levers, gears and sensors in one build.
research: how open-ended building affects engagement and persistence.
gesture, talk and handling of parts during group work.
comparing printed, video and peer-written build instructions.
notes: Medium difficulty — plan a first session around one guided build.
The expansion board has a rechargeable battery; charge it before a session.
Keep the parts sorted in the case compartments to make clean-up quick.

name: Omni One
lead: Virtuix omnidirectional VR treadmill — walk and run inside virtual worlds
caption: The Omni One platform with its support arm, installed in the lab.
summary: A full-body VR system: the user stands on a low-friction dish wearing special shoes and a support harness, and physically walks, runs or crouches to move through the virtual environment. Combined with a VR headset, it turns locomotion into a natural movement instead of a joystick push — which matters for presence, for exercise and for studies of embodied experience.
teaching: walking through a city, a museum, a historical site or a natural environment.
showing the difference between seated and full-body VR in media, design or technology courses.
research: comparing locomotion methods and their effect on learning or recall.
how different users navigate and orient themselves.
onboarding, comfort and motion sickness across users.
notes: Needs a clear area around the platform and a short safety briefing before use.
Sessions should be short at first; ask about dizziness and take breaks.
Users wear the Omni One vest and shoes; fit them before each session.

name: Pocketalk S2 Plus
lead: Handheld two-way voice and camera translator with a large touchscreen
caption: Our Pocketalk S2 Plus in its box, with the wall charger and cable.
summary: A phone-sized device built for one thing: translating conversations. Press the button, speak, and it shows and speaks the translation; hand it to the other person and it works the other way. The camera reads signs, menus and printed text and translates them on screen. The Plus model has an extra-large screen and a built-in eSIM, so it connects without Wi-Fi in more than 170 countries and regions; it covers more than 80 languages.
kit: translation runs online; check that the data plan is active before a session
teaching: students test the device with jargon, idioms and accents and analyse what it gets wrong.
Supporting multilingual learners in any class:
newcomer students follow instructions and join group work.
pre-service teachers role-play parent–teacher conferences across languages.
conversations with guest speakers or partner classes who speak another language.
research: how speakers adapt their talk when a device mediates the conversation.
systematic comparisons across languages, accents and registers.
use of translation devices with newcomer students and families.
notes: Recording other people's speech for translation still calls for consent; explain what the device does before using it with participants.
Do not rely on it for high-stakes exchanges (health, legal, grading) without a human check.

name: Portable Podcast Kit
lead: Movo MDX-2 bundle — two-person recording setup for computers, tablets and phones
caption: Our kit: two dynamic microphones on stands, the MDX-2 interface and two headphones.
summary: A compact two-channel recording setup that lets two speakers record clean, separate audio tracks on a laptop, tablet or phone — no studio required. The MDX-2 interface runs on batteries or USB power, so the kit can be carried to a classroom, an office or the field and set up in minutes. It suits podcasting, interviews, reflective audio journals and any project where students produce audio rather than only consume it.
kit: — 2 inputs, headphone monitoring, up to 24-bit/48 kHz; runs on USB power or 2 AA batteries
a recording device (any laptop, tablet or phone with a recording app such as Audacity or GarageBand)
teaching: explain a concept, debate an issue, review a book or report on a project.
with experts, community members or family — oral histories for social studies, careers for counselling.
students record what they learned and listen back at the end of the term.
two-voice narratives with sound effects and music.
recording and reviewing classroom talk and questioning.
research: clean two-track recordings for qualitative and oral-history research.
podcasts and audio journals as data on learning and reflection.
notes: Each microphone records to its own track; keep headphones on while recording and set gain so speech peaks around –12 dB.
Any phone, tablet or laptop with a recording app works — Audacity, GarageBand or Voice Memos are enough to start.
Dynamic microphones pick up little room noise, so ordinary classrooms work fine.

name: Ray-Ban Meta Smart Glasses
lead: Wayfarer (Gen 2) — camera, open-ear audio and a voice assistant in a pair of glasses
caption: One of the four pairs, with its charging case and box.
summary: Ordinary-looking glasses with a built-in camera, microphones and small speakers in the arms. The wearer can take first-person photos and video, listen to audio, take calls, and talk to the Meta AI assistant — asking what it sees, translating speech or text, or answering questions hands-free. They pair with a phone through the Meta AI app.

Meta AI app on a paired phone

name: RoboSapien
caption: The RoboSapien with its infrared remote.
summary: A humanoid robot that walks, dances, picks up objects and makes sounds and gestures, controlled by an infrared remote. It can be programmed with sequences of moves and reacts to touch and sound. More playful than the other robots in the lab, it is a strong hook for younger learners and for demonstrations of commands, sequences and body language.
kit: through the remote — sequence, touch-sensor and sound-sensor programs
teaching: students plan a routine step by step, then program it on the remote.
an engaging first contact for younger learners before the coding kits.
a short skit or presentation with the robot as a character.
what makes a machine seem alive, and how should we treat robots?
research: responses to a humanoid, non-speaking robot.
humanoid, screen-based and ball-shaped robots in learning activities.
notes: Programming is done entirely through the remote; the manual explains the sequence modes.

name: Sphero BOLT Power Pack
lead: 15 programmable robot balls with charging bases, protractors and an educator guide
caption: The BOLT Power Pack case with the 15 robots in their inductive charging bases.
summary: Sphero BOLT is a transparent, app-controlled robot ball with an 8×8 LED matrix, sensors (gyroscope, accelerometer, light, compass) and infrared communication between robots. Students drive it, draw paths for it, program it with blocks or JavaScript in the Sphero Edu app, and build activities around its sensors. The Power Pack holds fifteen robots, charging them in one case — enough for a whole class working in pairs.
